sets.title: Testing two water filters
sets.summary: Students name lab materials, compare two water filter designs and explain why one works better, then evaluate a plan to use a filter for drinking water, building cause-and-effect and claim-evidence language.

tasks.prompt: Look at the materials on the lab table. Name the things you see.
tasks.support: Words: beaker, muddy water, rocks, sand, cotton, timer.

visual.alt: A lab table with a beaker of muddy water, a cup of small rocks, a cup of sand, cotton balls and a timer

models.text: Beaker. Water. Rocks.
models.note: Discourse: a list of single words. Sentence: no sentences yet. Word: names lab objects, including the science word beaker.

models.text: I see a beaker with dirty water. There is rocks and sand. Also a timer.
models.note: Discourse: names most of the materials. Sentence: simple sentences, one agreement error (There is rocks) and one fragment. Word: uses dirty instead of muddy.

models.text: On the lab table there is a clear beaker full of muddy water, a cup of small rocks, some sand, a few cotton balls and a timer, so it looks like we are going to test ways to clean the water.
models.note: Discourse: lists the materials and predicts the purpose of the lab. Sentence: one long, well-built sentence with a series and so. Word: precise words like muddy, clear and test.

checklist: I named the materials.
I used describing words like muddy or small.
I used science words like beaker.

tasks.prompt: The class built two filters. Filter A has only rocks. Filter B has a layer of rocks, then a layer of sand, then cotton. The water that came out of Filter B was much clearer. Compare the two filters and explain why Filter B worked better.
tasks.support: Use: layer, particles, gaps, trap, clearer, while, because.

visual.alt: Two filters side by side: Filter A with only rocks and cloudy water below it, Filter B with rocks, sand and cotton and clearer water below it

models.text: Filter B clean. Sand. Rocks big holes.
models.note: Discourse: names the better filter and two key ideas. Sentence: phrases without verbs. Word: holes stands in for gaps.

models.text: Filter A only have rocks, and Filter B has rocks, sand and cotton. Filter B worked better because the sand is small and it catch the little dirt. The rocks have big spaces so the dirt go through.
models.note: Discourse: compares, then explains the cause. Sentence: uses because and so, with verb errors (have, catch, go). Word: everyday words like little dirt and big spaces for particles and gaps.

models.text: Both filters started with a layer of rocks, but Filter B also had sand and cotton underneath. Filter B produced clearer water because each layer traps smaller particles than the one above it. The gaps between the rocks are large, so fine mud slips right through Filter A, while the tiny spaces in the sand and the cotton fibers catch the particles the rocks miss.
models.note: Discourse: a clear comparison followed by a step-by-step cause. Sentence: uses but, because, so and while to show contrast and cause. Word: precise science words like particles, layer, fibers and produced.

checklist: I compared the two filters.
I explained why Filter B worked better.
I used science words like layer and particles.
I used because or while.

tasks.prompt: Filter B made clearer water, but it took 4 minutes. Filter A took only 1 minute. A team wants to use Filter B to clean stream water for drinking on a camping trip. Is that a good plan? Use evidence from the investigation to support your answer.
tasks.support: I think the plan is ___ because ___. The evidence shows ___. However, ___.

visual.alt: A stream in the mountains, a timer showing 4 minutes for Filter B, and a question mark

models.text: Filter B. Clean. But slow.
models.note: Discourse: a choice and one trade-off. Sentence: short phrases joined by but. Word: everyday words clean and slow.

models.text: I think Filter B is good because the water is more clear than Filter A. It is slow, but clean water is more important than fast water. But maybe they need to boil it too.
models.note: Discourse: a position, evidence, a trade-off and a new idea at the end. Sentence: uses because and but, with one error (more clear). Word: uses important and boil, but the boiling idea is not explained.

models.text: Filter B is a good first step, but it is not enough by itself. Our results show it removed far more mud than Filter A, so it is worth waiting the extra 3 minutes. However, clear water is not always safe water. A sand-and-cotton filter can trap dirt, but it cannot remove germs that are too small to see. So the team should use Filter B to clean the water and then boil it before drinking.
models.note: Discourse: a qualified claim, evidence from the test, a limit of the evidence and a recommendation. Sentence: uses so, however and but to build a careful argument. Word: precise words like results, removed, worth and germs.

checklist: I said if the plan is good.
I used evidence from the test.
I explained a limit or a problem with the plan.
I used words like however or but.

sets.title: Choosing a site for the center
sets.summary: Students describe two possible sites on a town map, compare their advantages, and argue for one site with reasons and a response to an opposing view.

tasks.prompt: The town will build a new community center. Look at the town map. Name the places you see near Site 1 and near Site 2.
tasks.support: Words: bus stop, stores, houses, park, downtown, edge of town.

visual.alt: A town map. Site 1 is downtown next to a bus stop and stores. Site 2 is at the edge of town next to new houses and a park.

models.text: Bus. Store. House. Park.
models.note: Discourse: a list of places. Sentence: no sentences yet. Word: common nouns, not yet linked to the two sites.

models.text: Site 1 is near the bus and the stores. Site 2 is near houses and a park.
models.note: Discourse: sorts the places by site. Sentence: two parallel sentences using is near. Word: uses the site names correctly.

models.text: Site 1 is downtown, right next to a bus stop and a row of stores. Site 2 is at the edge of town, surrounded by new houses and close to a park.
models.note: Discourse: contrasts the two sites clearly. Sentence: sentences with added detail phrases. Word: precise location words like downtown, surrounded by and edge of town.

checklist: I named places near each site.
I used the names Site 1 and Site 2.
I used location words like near or next to.

tasks.prompt: Compare the two sites. Tell one way Site 1 is better and one way Site 2 is better. Explain why each one matters for the people in the town.
tasks.support: Use: closer to, farther from, on the other hand, whereas, which means.

visual.alt: The town map with Site 1 by the bus stop and Site 2 by the park and houses, and people from the town

models.text: Site 1 bus. Easy go. Site 2 park. Families.
models.note: Discourse: one idea for each site. Sentence: phrases without verbs. Word: everyday words like easy go stand in for easy to reach.

models.text: Site 1 is better because it is close to the bus, so people with no car can go there. Site 2 is better because it is near the houses and the park, so families can walk. But Site 2 is far from the bus.
models.note: Discourse: an advantage for each site with a reason, and a disadvantage. Sentence: repeats one pattern with because and so; mostly correct. Word: uses close to and far from.

models.text: Site 1 has a clear advantage for transportation: it sits next to a bus stop, which means people who do not drive can reach it easily. Site 2, on the other hand, is closer to where many families actually live, and the nearby park would give the center outdoor space for programs. So Site 1 is easier to reach from across town, whereas Site 2 is more convenient for the neighborhood around it.
models.note: Discourse: a balanced comparison that ends with a summary. Sentence: uses which means, on the other hand and whereas to compare. Word: precise words like advantage, transportation and convenient.

checklist: I told one good thing about each site.
I explained why it matters to people.
I used compare words like whereas or on the other hand.

tasks.prompt: The town council will choose one site. Which site should they choose? State your position, give at least two reasons from the map, and respond to one reason someone might disagree with you.
tasks.support: I believe the council should choose ___. First, ___. In addition, ___. Some people might argue ___, but ___.

visual.alt: The town map, a group of council members, and a question mark between Site 1 and Site 2

models.text: Site 1. Bus. Many people. Stores.
models.note: Discourse: a choice and a list of reasons. Sentence: words and short phrases. Word: map words used as reasons.

models.text: I think the council should pick Site 1. First, it is next to the bus stop so anyone in town can go. Also there is stores near, so people can do shopping after. Some people say Site 2 have a park, but Site 1 is more fair for everybody.
models.note: Discourse: a position, two reasons and a short response to the other side. Sentence: uses first, also and but, with agreement errors (there is stores, Site 2 have). Word: uses fair, but does not explain why it is fairer.

models.text: I believe the council should choose Site 1. First, a community center should serve the whole town, and the bus stop means students, older adults and people without cars can all get there. In addition, the nearby stores already bring people downtown, so the center would get more visitors. Some people might argue that Site 2 is better because of the park and the new houses. That is a fair point, but those families could still take the bus downtown, while people across town would have no easy way to reach Site 2.
models.note: Discourse: a full argument with a claim, two reasons and a counterclaim that is answered. Sentence: uses in addition, might argue and while to connect and contrast. Word: precise words like serve and visitors, and polite phrases for answering the other side, like that is a fair point.

checklist: I stated my position.
I gave two reasons from the map.
I answered someone who might disagree.
I used words like first, in addition and but.

sets.title: Making trail mix for the class
sets.summary: Students read a recipe, explain how to scale it with a ratio, and evaluate a classmate's adding strategy, using ratio language to explain why multiplying keeps the mix the same.

tasks.prompt: Look at the recipe card for trail mix. Name the ingredients and say how many cups of each one the recipe uses.
tasks.support: Words: cups, cereal, dried apples, seeds, servings.

visual.alt: A recipe card for trail mix: 3 cups of cereal, 2 cups of dried apples, 1 cup of seeds. Makes 6 servings.

models.text: Cereal three. Apple two. Seeds one.
models.note: Discourse: names each ingredient with a number. Sentence: two-word phrases. Word: ingredient names and number words, without the word cups.

models.text: The recipe has 3 cups of cereal, 2 cups dried apple and 1 cup seeds. It make 6 servings.
models.note: Discourse: lists all ingredients and adds the servings. Sentence: correct first sentence with small errors (missing of, make). Word: uses cups and servings.

models.text: The recipe calls for 3 cups of cereal, 2 cups of dried apples and 1 cup of seeds, and the whole batch makes 6 servings.
models.note: Discourse: complete and organized in one statement. Sentence: one long, correct sentence with a series. Word: recipe language like calls for and batch.

checklist: I named the ingredients.
I said how many cups of each.
I said how many servings.

tasks.prompt: Your class needs 18 servings of trail mix. The recipe makes 6 servings. Explain, step by step, how you would change the recipe.
tasks.support: Use: divide, multiply, times, each, ratio, so.

visual.alt: A class of students, and the trail mix ingredients: cereal, dried apples and seeds

models.text: 18. Three times. Nine cereal.
models.note: Discourse: gives the key number and one result. Sentence: phrases only. Word: three times shows the idea of multiplying.

models.text: We need 18 servings and the recipe make 6, so 18 divide by 6 is 3. Then I multiply everything by 3. So 9 cups cereal, 6 cups apples and 3 cups seeds.
models.note: Discourse: clear steps in order with so and then. Sentence: mostly complete, with small errors (make, divide by). Word: uses multiply and divide.

models.text: First, I would figure out how many batches we need. Eighteen servings divided by 6 servings per batch is 3, so we need to triple the recipe. Then I would multiply each ingredient by 3: 9 cups of cereal, 6 cups of dried apples and 3 cups of seeds. That keeps the ratio of 3 to 2 to 1 the same, so the mix will taste the same.
models.note: Discourse: steps in order and a reason the method works. Sentence: uses first, then and so, with would for a plan. Word: precise math words like per batch, triple and ratio.

checklist: I explained the steps in order.
I said the new amounts.
I used math words like multiply or ratio.

tasks.prompt: Dani made the trail mix a different way. She added 2 more cups of each ingredient, so she used 5 cups of cereal, 4 cups of dried apples and 3 cups of seeds. Will her trail mix taste the same as the original? Will it make 18 servings? Explain your reasoning using ratios.
tasks.support: Dani's mix will / will not ___ because ___. The original ratio is ___, but ___. To fix it, ___.

visual.alt: Dani's trail mix with 5 cups of cereal, 4 cups of dried apples and 3 cups of seeds, next to a question mark

models.text: No. Not same. More seeds.
models.note: Discourse: an answer and one detail. Sentence: short phrases. Word: everyday words not same and more.

models.text: Dani's mix will not taste the same. The original is 3 to 2 to 1, but Dani's is 5 to 4 to 3, so it has too many seeds. Also it is only 12 cups, so it is not enough for 18 servings.
models.note: Discourse: answers both questions with evidence. Sentence: uses but, so and also; correct but repeats one pattern. Word: uses ratio form 3 to 2 to 1, but does not explain why adding changes it.

models.text: Dani's mix will not taste the same, and it will not be enough. Adding the same amount to each ingredient changes the ratio. In the original, cereal is half of the mix, 3 out of 6 cups, but in Dani's mix it is only 5 out of 12, which is less than half, and the seeds jump from one-sixth to one-fourth of the mix. Also, the recipe makes 1 cup per serving, so her 12 cups would only make 12 servings. To keep the flavor, she has to multiply each amount by the same number, not add.
models.note: Discourse: a two-part claim, detailed evidence, and a general rule as a fix. Sentence: uses which, but and so to link reasoning steps. Word: precise math language like out of, one-sixth, per serving and multiply by the same number.

checklist: I said if the mix will taste the same.
I said if it makes 18 servings.
I used ratios to explain.
I said how Dani could fix it.
